# 1. Introduction

We use normal data to illustrate how the similarity structure (SS) changes as the difference between two means increases. We then compare the resulting similarity sizes, `nS`, using the similar effect probability, `pS`.

The default settings reproduce the results and figures using estimates included in the package. Set `calculate_ss: true` to repeat the full subsampling analysis. This takes considerably longer.

# 2. Data and parameters

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5)
```

```{r data}
library(similaritystructure)
library(ggplot2)

# Use the same normal observations in each scenario, shifting the mean.
set.seed(12345)
x <- rnorm(20000, mean = 0, sd = 1)
mean_shift <- seq(0.05, 1.20, by = 0.05)

alpha <- 0.05
N_init <- 2
num_N <- 60
num_repet <- 300
seed <- 12345

stopifnot(params$test %in% c("ks-test", "t-test"))

# The upper subsample size decreases as the mean difference increases.
N_fin <- round(80 / mean_shift^2)
```

The second sample is `x + mean_shift`, so every scenario has exactly the specified mean difference and the same empirical spread. This design holds the underlying observations fixed across scenarios; the two original vectors are therefore not independent samples. Subsampling is performed with replacement. The example illustrates the behavior of the method under controlled shifts.

The selected test is `r params$test`, with 60 subsample sizes and 300 repetitions at each size.

# 3. Similarity structures

A single comparison can be estimated with `similarity_structure()`. For example, this is the call for a mean difference of 0.4:

```{r single-comparison, eval=FALSE}
res <- similarity_structure(
  x, x + 0.4, N_init = 2, N_fin = round(80 / 0.4^2),
  num_N = 60, num_repet = 300, replace = TRUE,
  test = "ks-test", alpha = 0.05, seed = 12345,
  plotting = FALSE
)
```

The complete analysis consists of the same calculation for all 24 mean differences. By default we load the saved estimates to avoid repeating the tests.

```{r similarity-structures}
source(system.file("scripts", "example_cache.R",
                   package = "similaritystructure"))

if (isTRUE(params$calculate_ss)) {

  ss <- list()
  dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)

  for (i in seq_along(mean_shift)) {
    delta <- mean_shift[i]

    ss[[as.character(delta)]] <- similarity_structure(
      x, x + delta,
      N_init = N_init, N_fin = N_fin[i],
      num_N = num_N, num_repet = num_repet,
      replace = TRUE, test = params$test,
      alpha = alpha, seed = seed, plotting = FALSE
    )
  }

  saveRDS(ss, file.path("results",
                       paste0("normal_", params$test, ".rds")))

} else {

  ss <- read_example_cache("mean", test = params$test)
}

# Two example results, for differences of 0.2 and 0.4
A <- ss[["0.2"]]$simil_struct_Ns
B <- ss[["0.4"]]$simil_struct_Ns

# The scaled non-rejection curve is not yet the normalized SS.
head(ss[["0.4"]]$scaled_bn)
```

## Empirical curves and approximations

Black lines show the empirical, scaled non-rejection probability. Red lines show the parametric fit; green lines show the binomial GAM. Vertical lines indicate the corresponding similarity sizes.

```{r empirical-curves, fig.width=14, fig.height=10}
op <- par(mfrow = c(4, 6), mar = c(3, 3, 1.6, 0.5), cex = 0.8)

for (delta in mean_shift) {
  x_ss <- ss[[as.character(delta)]]
  empirical <- x_ss$scaled_bn
  fit <- x_ss$simil_struct_Ns$fitting
  smooth <- x_ss$simil_struct_Ns$smooth

  plot(empirical$N, empirical$scaled, type = "l",
       xlab = "Subsample size", ylab = "Scaled beta(n)",
       main = paste("Shift =", delta))
  if (!is.null(fit)) {
    lines(fit$vect_N_fit, fit$fun_fit, col = "firebrick", lwd = 1.5)
    abline(v = fit$Ns_fitting, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
  }
  lines(smooth$vect_N_smooth, smooth$fun_smooth,
        col = "darkgreen", lwd = 1.5)
  abline(v = smooth$Ns_smooth, col = "darkgreen", lty = 2)
}

par(op)
```

# 4. Similarity size

The similarity size is the expected subsample size under the normalized SS. We report both estimation approaches.

```{r similarity-sizes}
ns <- data.frame(Mean_shift = mean_shift,
                 Fitting = NA_real_, Smoothing = NA_real_)

for (i in seq_along(mean_shift)) {
  result <- ss[[as.character(mean_shift[i])]]$simil_struct_Ns
  if (!is.null(result$fitting)) ns$Fitting[i] <- result$fitting$Ns_fitting
  ns$Smoothing[i] <- result$smooth$Ns_smooth
}

print(ns, row.names = FALSE, digits = 5)

# Inspect the two similarity sizes from the selected example.
c(Fitting = B$fitting$Ns_fitting, GAM = B$smooth$Ns_smooth)
```

## Normalized similarity structures

The following curves represent `S(n)`, not the scaled non-rejection probabilities. Both panels use a logarithmic x-axis.

```{r normalized-curves, fig.width=11, fig.height=5}
colors <- grDevices::hcl.colors(length(mean_shift), "Spectral")
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

for (method in c("fitting", "smooth")) {
  plot(2, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(2, 1000), ylim = c(0, 0.11),
       log = "x", xlab = "Subsample size (n)", ylab = "S(n)",
       main = if (method == "fitting") "Parametric fitting" else "Binomial GAM")

  for (i in rev(seq_along(mean_shift))) {
    result <- ss[[as.character(mean_shift[i])]]$simil_struct_Ns[[method]]
    if (is.null(result)) next

    n <- if (method == "fitting") result$vect_N_fit else result$vect_N_smooth
    lines(n, result$Sn, col = colors[i], lwd = 1.4)
  }
}

par(op)
```

# 5. Comparing similarity structures with pS

The function `prob_effect()` compares two normalized similarity structures. Here we compare mean shifts of 0.2 and 0.4.

```{r one-ps}
prob_effect(fitting_A = A$fitting, fitting_B = B$fitting)
prob_effect(smooth_A = A$smooth, smooth_B = B$smooth)
```

We can also compare all 24 effects pairwise. The matrix is symmetric and its diagonal is left blank, since we are interested in comparisons between different effects.

```{r ps-matrices}
labels <- as.character(mean_shift)
n <- length(labels)
ps_fit <- ps_smooth <- matrix(NA_real_, n, n,
                              dimnames = list(labels, labels))

for (i in 1:(n - 1)) {
  for (j in (i + 1):n) {
    first <- ss[[labels[i]]]$simil_struct_Ns
    second <- ss[[labels[j]]]$simil_struct_Ns

    if (!is.null(first$fitting) && !is.null(second$fitting)) {
      ps_fit[i, j] <- prob_effect(fitting_A = first$fitting,
                                 fitting_B = second$fitting)
      ps_fit[j, i] <- ps_fit[i, j]
    }

    ps_smooth[i, j] <- prob_effect(smooth_A = first$smooth,
                                   smooth_B = second$smooth)
    ps_smooth[j, i] <- ps_smooth[i, j]
  }
}
```

```{r ps-figure, fig.width=13, fig.height=6}
ps_plot <- rbind(
  data.frame(as.table(ps_fit), Method = "Fitting"),
  data.frame(as.table(ps_smooth), Method = "Binomial GAM")
)
names(ps_plot)[1:3] <- c("Shift_A", "Shift_B", "pS")
ps_plot$Shift_A <- factor(ps_plot$Shift_A, levels = labels)
ps_plot$Shift_B <- factor(ps_plot$Shift_B, levels = rev(labels))

ggplot(ps_plot, aes(x = Shift_A, y = Shift_B, fill = pS)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_wrap(~Method) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey90") +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Mean shift", y = "Mean shift", fill = "pS") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

# 6. Reproducibility

The included estimates allow quick reproduction of the figures. To repeat the full analysis, set `calculate_ss: true` in the document header or use:

```{r rerun, eval=FALSE}
rmarkdown::render(
  "example_01_mean.Rmd",
  params = list(calculate_ss = TRUE, test = "ks-test")
)
```

Use `test: "t-test"` to reproduce the corresponding t-test example. With replacement, large subsample sizes can contain repeated observations; they do not represent additional independent participants. The reported `pS` is a descriptive comparison probability, not a hypothesis-test p-value.
